beneficiaries_note: Founds charities: each charity it launched, read live, brings its own countries.
summary: Ambitious Impact (formerly Charity Entrepreneurship) researches intervention ideas and founds new charities to run the best of them; this model covers all its programmes in the year to March 2025: the nine charities and five effective giving organisations it launched, Founding to Give, its funding circles, grantmaker and research training, and its research, against its own spending of $2.5M (the seed grants it passed on are valued as money for the new charities). At the defaults it averts about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000: each charity founded is credited with the average lifetime fundraising of its charities ($107M raised by 60 so far, times 2.5 for the years to come), 60% of it caused by Ambitious Impact, valued at the figures the rankings give the charities it has launched, institutional funders' grants as all shifted and the rest half new money, each effective giving organisation and Founding to Give company with the donations it is expected to move, at GiveWell's Top Charities, less the giving organisations' running costs, the giving organisations' part at Ambitious Impact's share of the credit ({{row:egi_credit_share}}; the organisation that asks the donor takes the rest); the next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the past average. It creates charities that each go on to raise and spend several times its cost per charity, most of them in global health. The result moves most with the missing-data discount, where shifted money would otherwise have gone, the discount rate and the next-dollar figure; the projected part of its charities' future fundraising, the giving organisations' and companies' donations, the spending its grantmaker training and research changed and its fellows' careers are discounted for missing data.

resources.title: Charity Entrepreneurship (Ambitious Impact), charity 1195850, Trustees' Report and Audited Financial Statements, year ended 31 March 2025 (Moore Kingston Smith LLP; filed copy of the Charity Commission's register)

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

rows.label: Money raised since 2019 by the charities it launched, in the prices of each year (US$)

source.title: Ambitious Impact, Our charities
source.quote: $107M+ raised since 2019 by charities launched through Ambitious Impact

rows.explainer: Everything its charities have raised from all funders (GiveWell, Open Philanthropy, the Animal Welfare Fund, funding circles, individual donors, its own seed grants), its own count, unaudited. Raised is close to spent for small charities without endowments. Its own seed grants (about $1.3M in the year modelled) are a small part of it.

rows.label: Money raised since 2019 by the charities it launched, in 2024 prices (US$)
rows.explainer: The nominal sum brought to 2024 prices at 2023, about the money-weighted middle of the years 2019 to 2025 (most of the money came after 2021, as the cohorts grew and GiveWell began funding them) (Convention 8).

rows.label: Charities it has launched since 2018
rows.explainer: Its own count, "60+": 60 as stated (more would lower the average a little). Includes those that have closed, so the average below counts failures.

rows.label: Money raised so far per charity launched, failures included (US$)
rows.explainer: About {{row:raised_per_charity_to_date}} per charity: an average over every cohort since 2018, the ones that closed and the young ones that have barely started included. This part of a new charity's money is measured: what its predecessors raised.

rows.label: A launched charity's lifetime fundraising as a multiple of the average raised so far
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The average so far stops at today: the charities are on average about three years old (cohorts of 6 to 10 a year since 2018, most of them since 2021), and the ones that survive grow (Fortify Health, Suvita, Family Empowerment Media, Shrimp Welfare Project and Ansh now spend $1M to $5M a year; GiveWell has funded 13). A charity's whole life raises more than its first three years: 2.5 times (1.5 if most of the money comes from a few charities whose growth has peaked, 5 if the survivors keep growing for a decade, as Fortify Health has since 2018). Closures are in the multiple: the failed ones add nothing further. The part beyond what has been raised so far is a projection and takes the missing-data step (founded_projected_missing_data_adj).

rows.label: Years from launch to the middle of the money a charity raises in its first years
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The part measured by its past charities is what the average one has raised so far, at an average age of about three years, most of it in the first years after a seed grant of $150,000 to $190,000: its middle comes about 1.5 years after launch (1 to 3).

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the charities spend the measured part
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Years from launch to the middle of the money a charity raises after its first years
rows.explainer: No published study tracks how a new charity's fundraising is spread over its life, so there is no reference class; our judgment from the model's own timeline. The projected part comes after the first three years, as the survivors scale: its middle about six years after launch (four if growth stops early, nine if it lasts a decade). Drawn together with the lifetime multiple: a charity that keeps growing raises more and later.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the charities spend the projected part
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Share of each founded organisation's existence that wouldn't have happened without the programme
rows.explainer: Our judgment, of one question: would the organisation exist anyway, then or soon after? Its research picks ideas no organisation is running at scale (its idea reports assess who else works on each idea), it recruits and trains the founders, many of them not planning to found a charity, pairs them and finds the seed money (about 95% of proposals funded); against that, some ideas were already being pursued in some form (lead paint, tobacco taxes, kangaroo care), some founders would have started something on their own, and a charity started a few years later is partly the same charity. 60% (30% to 85%). No study measures it. Anchors: the site's other counterfactual shares for meta work, a meta charity's own effect on donations it records (30%, 15% to 45%, @meta.own_effect_share) and the share of career changes a programme caused (30%, 10% to 60%); higher here because the programme supplies the idea, the team and the seed money together. The founders' own alternative work is not a question of this row: their forgone pay is credited, by share of resources, in the founded charities' own models.

rows.label: Money the year's charities will raise, the part measured by its past charities, caused by it, discounted (US$)
rows.explainer: Each charity at what the average charity it launched has raised so far (closures included), discounted for the wait, times the share of its existence the programme caused.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity (the projected part of the founded money)
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the money its charities will raise beyond what the average has raised so far is a projection by judgment (lifetime_vs_to_date), not a count.

rows.label: Money the year's charities will raise beyond that, projected, caused by it, discounted (US$)
rows.explainer: The rest of a charity's lifetime fundraising (the lifetime multiple less the part raised so far), on the same steps with its own wait, and the missing-data step.

rows.label: Money the charities it founded in the year will raise and spend, caused by it, discounted (US$)
rows.explainer: The measured and the projected part. Valued below as money moved, at the figures of the charities it founds: the institutional funders' part all shifted, the rest half new money.

rows.label: Share of its charities' money that comes from institutional funders (GiveWell, Open Philanthropy, other foundations and funds)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. GiveWell gave $7.5M to five of its charities in the year (accounts p. 17), $7M of GiveWell grants have gone to Ansh and more than $5M to Taimaka (Ambitious Impact, Our charities), and Open Philanthropy, the Animal Welfare Fund and the funding circles fund most of the rest; individual donors give the remainder. 60% (40% to 80%). Such funders' money would have been granted anyway, so it is valued as all shifted (shifted_dollar_value), as Open Philanthropy's money is in our model of GiveWell.

rows.label: Grants made through the funding circles it runs, in the year (US$)

source.title: Charity Entrepreneurship (Ambitious Impact), charity 1195850, Trustees' Report and Audited Financial Statements, year ended 31 March 2025 (Moore Kingston Smith LLP; filed copy of the Charity Commission's register)
source.quote: we facilitated a total of $5.8 million in charitable funding to high-impact organizations

rows.explainer: Its funding circles (groups of funders pooling grants, among them the Sustainable Animal Welfare circle, $650,000, and the Mental Health circle, $1.8 million) granted $5.8M in the year (p. 14: "resulted in $5.8 million USD being granted"), to its own charities and others.

rows.label: Share of the funding circles' grants that its organising caused
rows.explainer: The site's shared own-effect share for money a meta charity records without a donor survey of its own (30%, 15% to 45%). The members are established funders who would have granted the money anyway, so it is all shifted. Circle grants to its own charities are credited here and again in their fundraising (at founding_counterfactual_share); the two shares together stay below 100% of the money, and the circles' grant lists aren't published to separate them. Valued at the mix of the charities it founds (shifted_dollar_value): the circles fund its own charities and other high-impact ones in global health, mental health and animal welfare, as its own charities do.

rows.label: Donations an effective giving organisation it launched records over its life, if it succeeds (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Each is a national platform taking tax-deductible donations for effective charities (Belgium and the Netherlands, France, Italy and others). FarmKind, a giving platform from an earlier cohort, has raised almost $4M for its recommended charities (Ambitious Impact, Our charities); national platforms in smaller markets record less, and the largest established one, Effektiv Spenden in Germany and Switzerland (founded 2019; its 2025 transparency page, quoted in facts/meta.json: "fast 30 Millionen Euro" a year), is far above a typical one. $2M over its life ($0.5M to $10M), recorded donations before its own effect.

rows.label: Chance that a new effective giving organisation succeeds
rows.explainer: The site's one chance of success for a new, not-yet-proven meta organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.8).

rows.label: Expected share of the donations a successful one records, success or failure
rows.explainer: The shared success step for the money: one that fails still moves @meta.failure_money_share of what it would have moved. Its costs are Ambitious Impact's programme spending, counted in full whichever way it goes.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity (the effective giving organisations' future donations)
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the five organisations' donations are a projection by judgment (egi_moved_per_org), not a count.

rows.label: Its share of the credit for the donations its effective giving organisations move
rows.explainer: The site's one split for a dollar two organisations both moved (docs/normalization.md 2.24, overlap): the giving organisation asks the donor and takes the donor's side, Ambitious Impact, which founded it, the rest, {{row:egi_credit_share}}. A different step from the share of their existence it caused, which removes what would have happened anyway.

rows.label: Donations its effective giving organisations will move, caused by them and by it, discounted (US$)
rows.formula: egi_orgs_launched * egi_moved_per_org * egi_success_adj * @meta.own_effect_share * projected_wait_discount * founding_counterfactual_share * egi_missing_data_adj
rows.explainer: Organisations × recorded donations × the success step × their own effect on the donations (the site's shared share for a meta charity without its own donor survey, 30%) × the wait (the middle of their giving about six years on, as for the charities' projected money) × the share of their existence the programme caused × the missing-data step.

rows.label: Donations its effective giving organisations will move, credited to Ambitious Impact (US$)
rows.explainer: The giving organisation and the incubator that founded it both moved these donations; Ambitious Impact takes its share of the credit.

rows.label: An effective giving organisation's own spending over its life, success or failure (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. A national giving platform run by one or two staff and volunteers spends about $50,000 to $150,000 a year; one that fails closes after about three years (@meta.failure_years_run), one that succeeds runs for a decade or more: $0.5M expected over its life ($0.15M to $1.5M). Paid by donors who would otherwise have given it to effective charities, it is subtracted at where that money would have gone (egi_costs_value).

rows.label: Companies launched by its Founding to Give programme in the year

source.title: Charity Entrepreneurship (Ambitious Impact), charity 1195850, Trustees' Report and Audited Financial Statements, year ended 31 March 2025 (Moore Kingston Smith LLP; filed copy of the Charity Commission's register)

rows.explainer: January to April 2025: for-profit start-ups whose founders commit to give a large share of what the companies earn them to effective charities.

rows.label: Expected donations per Founding to Give company, undiscounted (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, built from a reference chain: about one start-up in ten reaches an exit or profits that pay its founders well within a decade; such a modest exit leaves two founders a few million dollars between them after dilution (about $3M); and the founders give perhaps half of it. 0.1 × $3M × 0.5 ≈ $150,000 per company ($15,000 if exits are rarer and smaller, $1.5M if one company in the cohort becomes a large success, which dominates the mean). Before discounting. No company had given anything by the end of the year.

rows.label: Years until a Founding to Give company's founders give
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a start-up's exit or profits come, if at all, about a decade after founding (5 to 15 years).

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the companies' founders give
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity (Founding to Give's donations)
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the companies' donations are a projection by judgment (f2g_donations_per_company); none has given yet.

rows.label: Donations its Founding to Give companies will make, caused by it (US$)
rows.explainer: Companies × expected donations × the discounted wait × the share of their existence the programme caused (the same share as for its charities: it recruits, trains and pairs the founders) × the missing-data step. Valued, like the giving organisations' money, at GiveWell's Top Charities, half of it counted new by the shared rule.

rows.label: Donations moved to effective charities by its effective giving organisations and Founding to Give companies, caused by it (US$)
rows.explainer: Both raise money from people for effective charities, chiefly GiveWell's: valued at GiveWell's Top Charities (value_global_health), half new money (gh_moved_dollar_net_value).

rows.label: Money individual donors give to the charities it founded, caused by it (US$)
rows.explainer: Individual donors' part of its charities' money, valued through the shared rows for money moved at its charities' figures: half new money, half shifted (@meta.new_money_share).

rows.label: Money institutional funders give to its charities and through its circles because of it, all shifted (US$)
rows.explainer: Grants funders would have made anyway, now to its charities: they count only for the gain over where they would have gone (shifted_dollar_value).

rows.label: Money raised for effective charities that it caused, per dollar of its cost
rows.explainer: Context.

rows.label: Yearly grants of the grantmakers its Impactful Grantmaking Program trained (US$)

source.title: Charity Entrepreneurship (Ambitious Impact), charity 1195850, Trustees' Report and Audited Financial Statements, year ended 31 March 2025 (Moore Kingston Smith LLP; filed copy of the Charity Commission's register)
source.quote: training 14 grantmakers who collectively control approximately $40 million per year

rows.explainer: Grantmakers at foundations and family offices, trained in its programme in the year.

rows.label: Share of those grants its training moves to better uses each year
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Most of a trained grantmaker's portfolio is set by the foundation's mandate; training changes how some grants are chosen (cost-effectiveness, evidence, neglected areas). 1.5% of a year's grants (0.5% to 4%), for each year it lasts (grantmaking_years). Anchor: Ambitious Impact's own estimate of about $3M of counterfactual value from the cohort (p. 17), 7.5% of $40M over the training's life, before any discount for its self-assessment; Rethink Priorities' research is credited 3% to 5% of the money it informs (our model of it).

rows.label: Years the training keeps changing a grantmaker's grants
rows.explainer: No study follows how long a grantmaking course changes the grants made afterwards, so there is no reference class. Grantmakers move on and practices drift back: about three years (one to five).

rows.label: Money outside its own incubation its published research informs in a year (US$)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Its research team recommended 12 ideas in the year (p. 10), with public reports and cost-effectiveness analyses. Most of that work feeds its own incubation (counted above, its cost in program_spend); others read it too: funders sizing grants to the new charities and to ideas others run, and other incubators and researchers. $5M a year informed ($1M to $20M).

rows.label: Share of that money its research moved to better uses
rows.explainer: Our judgment: a report sharpens or redirects a small part of the grants that read it.

rows.label: Spending its grantmaker training and research changed, in the year (US$)
rows.explainer: Money informed × the share changed, for both (the training's over its years, discounted at the shared rate). All shifted: these funders would have granted the money anyway, so it counts only for the gain over where it would have gone (informed_money_value). The money raised that it caused is in raised_money.
rows.formula: grantmakers_budget * grantmaking_share_changed * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, grantmaking_years) + research_money_informed * research_share_changed

rows.label: Value of a dollar to the charities it founds (its charities on the rankings, live), units of value
rows.explainer: The charities it has launched that the site ranks, each at its figure on the rankings (its primary evaluator's: GiveWell for Suvita, Family Empowerment Media, Fortify Health, Ansh, Taimaka, Lafiya Nigeria, Notify Health, Healthy Futures Global, Clear Solutions and Spiro; the Happier Lives Institute for ACTRA; charityevals' own models of what Learning Alliance, NOVAH, Oxygen Access Project, Respira Health, LABRI, Lead Research for Action, ARMoR, First Embrace and Kaya Guides have delivered; Animal Charity Evaluators for Shrimp Welfare Project), equal weights within each cause, and the two causes in the shares of the charities it founded in the year (eight in human well-being, one in animal welfare: Scale Welfare). Its charities without a model here (the youngest, whose only figure is Ambitious Impact's estimate from before they existed, which never ranks; LEEP, whose only model is unpublished, FarmKind, Rahi Impact, Scale Welfare, Radius, the Institute for Development Innovation and others) are valued at the average of their cause; its meta charities (CEARCH, Better Futures Guide) and the effective giving organisations at the average of the rest. Equal weights, not money weights: the charities that raised most (GiveWell's grantees) would weigh more by money.

rows.label: Value of a dollar its giving organisations and companies move, units of value
rows.explainer: A second destination set, gh (docs/normalization.md 2.8): the money its effective giving organisations and Founding to Give companies move goes to global health and poverty charities, so it is valued at that shared destination (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), while the charities it founds include animal ones.

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money to global-health charities would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: The shared prior of the gh destination set (docs/normalization.md 2.8): GiveDirectly's live result times the shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.label: Share of money moved that is new money
rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar to global health and poverty charities (GiveWell's Top Charities, live), units of value
rows.explainer: GiveWell's four Top Charities (Against Malaria Foundation, Malaria Consortium, Helen Keller Intl, New Incentives), each at GiveWell's figure for the charity on the rankings (its programmes and locations weighted by funding) under your values, weighted by what GiveWell directed to each in 2024 (50%, 29%, 18%, 4%).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, units of value
rows.explainer: Valued by where this organisation's money went: its own published split, each recipient at its live result on this site (value_destinations).

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: an ordinary charity of each cause its money goes to, in its own mix), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the shared rule for an organisation whose money goes to several causes. Shifted money would have gone to an ordinary charity of the same cause: each cause's at the rule for a mover in that cause (GiveDirectly's live result, times a shared multiple, 1×, from 0 to 3×, over the global-health charities' on the rankings, times that cause's charities'), weighted by the organisation's own split, all live under your values.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): the charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work.

rows.label: Value of a dollar all shifted (given anyway, now to a better use), at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: Money that would have been given or spent anyway counts only for the gain over where it would have gone: a grantmaker's grants, or spending that research or advice changed. Its owners spent it, so the organisation is credited its share of that gain (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of the spending its research or advice changed (all shifted money), units of value
rows.explainer: Spending its research or advice changed, at a judged share of the money it informed: all of it would have been spent anyway, so it counts for the gain over where it would have gone, discounted for weak evidence and for an outcome not measured for this charity (docs/normalization.md 2.8, 2.12).

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone. The donors gave it, so the organisation is credited its share of that good (mobiliser_share).

rows.label: Value of a dollar its giving organisations and companies move, net of where shifted money would have gone, at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: The shared net value of a dollar moved, in the gh destination set (docs/normalization.md 2.8): new money in full, shifted money for its gain over where it would have gone, at the mobiliser's share (2.24).

rows.label: Value lost to the effective giving organisations' own running costs (units of value)
rows.formula: egi_orgs_launched * egi_budget_per_org * projected_wait_discount * founding_counterfactual_share * egi_credit_share * gh_prior_dollar_value * mobiliser_share
rows.explainer: Their lifetime spending, on the same wait and counterfactual share as their donations, at where that money would otherwise have gone (an ordinary global-health charity), at Ambitious Impact's share of the credit for their donations and the mobiliser's share: a cost of the money they move, it takes the same shares as that money (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: People or animals per year the policy or research would affect
rows.explainer: 0: Ambitious Impact wins no policy itself; the policy work of the charities it founds is in their own figures, read through the destinations.

rows.label: Value per unit affected per year, in units of value
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Probability the change happens because of this work
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (Your values → How impact is counted; docs/normalization.md 2.9). Never the charity's or an evaluator's own years.

rows.label: Years from the win until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: Unused: the policy branch is 0 (units_affected_per_year), so this row multiplies nothing. It keeps the template's figure and range only so the canonical row exists; changing it moves no result.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the policy takes effect
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate, like every future benefit.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
Expected value of the policy or research (before adjustments)
Side benefits of its work beyond what the branches count, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Good the branches leave out: founders trained who later lead other organisations, the ideas and open cost-effectiveness analyses other charities and governments use, new markets its charities open (shrimp stunning equipment, fortified flour) that others enter. +8% (0% to +25%): small, since most of its research's use is already counted through its own charities.

rows.label: Side harms of its work beyond what the branches count, as a share of its value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Harm the branches leave out: staff time of governments, hospitals and partners its charities that fail used, and the attention of officials taken from other work. −2% (−8% to 0%). The founders' forgone pay is credited by share of resources in the founded charities' own models, not here.

rows.label: Value of the money it caused to be raised and the spending it changed (units of value)
rows.formula: (raised_money * moved_dollar_net_value + shifted_money * shifted_dollar_value + gh_money_moved * gh_moved_dollar_net_value - egi_costs_value + informed_money_value) * (1 + founding_side_benefits + founding_side_harms)
rows.explainer: The money individual donors and its companies give because of it, net of where shifted money would have gone; the institutional funders' and circles' grants, all shifted, at their gain; the giving organisations' and companies' donations at GiveWell's Top Charities, net, less the giving organisations' running costs; the spending its training and research changed, all shifted, with its evidence and missing-data steps; then the side effects.

rows.explainer: A further dollar: the share it grants to its new charities at their figures, the rest at its own work's past average, credited by share of resources and scaled to the next dollar.
